introduction: The guide begins far from any list, with a counsel for one person facing another: be friends with whoever strikes you, and return honey for poison. Only then come the principles, named by ‘Abdu’l-Bahá in one combination after another for a Paris gathering, an American journal, an ambassador, a group of missionaries: the search for truth, one human family under one Shepherd, religion as a cause of love and in accord with science, the equality of women and men, schooling for all, a common language, a tribunal, peace. All forty-six of the guide’s quotations are read here, and beside them forty-six passages from other scriptures, from philosophers, poets and public life. Many are near neighbours. The Qur’an also repels evil with what is better; Zamenhof proposed a second language for everyone in nearly the reading’s words; Eisenhower counted what arms cost the hungry; Tennyson’s prince says that woman and man rise or sink together, and Pope that a life in the right matters more than modes of faith. Others stand across the path. Confucius would answer injury with justice, Burke cherishes old prejudices because they are old, Santayana says that those who forget the past repeat it, Mill fears one school for all, Pericles calls the citizen who keeps out of politics useless, and the Preacher doubts that anything is new. Still others mark what a principle leaves open: Bacon and Pascal on how far reason reaches, Paine on where independent inquiry may end, Genesis on what one language once led to. The company is there so that each principle is met as a claim someone has disputed and someone else has shared, and not only as an item in a list.
questions: The guide opens by returning friendship for blows and honey for poison. The Qur’an promises that an enemy so treated may become a friend; Confucius asks what is then left to repay kindness with. How does this opening counsel bear on the social principles that follow it?

Independent investigation of truth stands first in many of these lists, with the abandonment of blind imitation. Set it beside Emerson, Paul’s “Prove all things”, Burke’s defence of inherited judgment and Santayana on those who cannot remember the past. What should a person who searches independently still take from those who came before?

Religion, the readings say, must agree with science and reason and must cause love, or it is better to be without it. Bacon, Tennyson and the two sayings of Pascal each draw the line between reason and faith differently, and Paine’s inquiry led him out of every church. Where do the readings draw it?

The readings ask whether any earlier book taught these principles; the Preacher says there is no new thing under the sun, and Paul had written that there is neither male nor female in Christ. What would make a teaching new: its words, its scope, or its being carried out?

One language, one curriculum, a supreme tribunal and non-interference in politics appear among the teachings. Mill, the story of Babel, the Qur’an’s verse on the difference of tongues and Pericles each raise a difficulty. Which difficulty seems to you most serious, and how might the readings answer it?

‘Abdu’l-Bahá gives the principles as twelve, as ten commandments, as a few words for an ambassador, and as five things to realize daily, and says, “You must act in accordance with these teachings.” Reading the whole with James, Micah and Pope, are the principles better understood as a programme for the world or as a way of living, and can they be one without the other?

outside.why: The reading answers blows with friendship and poison with honey. The Qur’an gives the same counsel as a rule with a promise attached: repel an evil deed with a better one, and the enemy may become as a bosom friend. The reading promises no such result; it asks for the remedy whatever the other does.

Asked about the very principle the reading teaches, that injury be repaid with kindness, Confucius asks what is then left to repay kindness with, and answers injury with justice. If the one who offers poison receives honey, what does the one who offers honey receive?

The reading’s sheep of God under one kind Shepherd is the Gospel’s image, and this verse already looks beyond the present flock to “other sheep”. In John they are to be brought to hear one voice; the reading says that all human beings are the flock already.

“Every era hath a spirit”, the reading says, and finds this era’s in a set of teachings. Lowell, writing against slavery in 1845, puts the same thought as a duty: what was good once grows uncouth, and whoever would keep up with truth must move.

The reading wants society “freed from the darkness of continually repeating the past”, and finds the cause in blind imitation. Santayana names the opposite cause: it is those who do not retain the past who repeat it, and progress depends on retentiveness. Can a mind search independently and still keep what was learned before it?

The first principle here promotes peace so that people “may be relieved from the burden of exorbitant expenditures”. A general who had become president counted that burden in 1953: every gun is a theft from the hungry and the cold. He speaks as the head of one armed power to another; the reading charges an institution with ending the cost.

The second principle would reduce languages to one, taught in every school. In Genesis one language is where humanity began, and its confounding is God’s answer to what a united people might build. What must go with a common tongue for the reading’s third principle, fellowship and kindliness, to follow from it?

The reading’s unity of language means that everyone would know two, “one’s native tongue and the universal language”. Zamenhof had made the same proposal, in nearly the same words, when he published Esperanto in 1887, as an oculist in Warsaw without a religion’s authority behind him.

The reading sets “the abandonment of ancient traditions” beside the search for reality, and the giving up of prejudices beside peace. Burke defends both things by name: an inherited judgment holds the wisdom of ages, and one person’s private stock of reason is small. Which of the prejudices the reading lists would Burke’s argument protect, and which not?

The reading says a peace plan failed because peace cannot stand “on a firm and lasting foundation” without religious power. The psalm says as much of any house or city: without the Lord the builders labour and the watchman wakes in vain.

The reading holds that peace must rest on the principles and not the principles on peace. UNESCO’s founders, after a second world war, also looked beneath treaties, and placed the defences of peace in the minds of men; they name education, science and culture where the reading names a divine power. Is that the same foundation under another name, or a different one?

The reading counts “obedience to just government” among the teachings. Thoreau, jailed for refusing a tax that paid for slavery and war, takes up the case the word “just” leaves open: where the government is unjust, he says, the just man belongs in its prison. Who decides when obedience is still owed?

The reading calls crafts, trade and farming forms of worship: the farmer in his field is like one who prays in a temple. Herbert had said it of the humblest work in an English hymn: a room swept “as for Thy laws” is made fine, and drudgery divine.

The reading asks “the voluntary sharing by the wealthy with the poor, not through force and coercion”. Paul, collecting for the poor of Jerusalem, sets the same condition: each as he purposes in his heart, not grudgingly or of necessity.

“Speak of the teachings … not of beliefs”, the reading advises, since that is what brings progress. Pope’s couplet makes the same choice: creeds are for zealots to fight over, and a life that is right cannot be wrong. Pope leaves it there; the reading’s list ends with a need no conduct supplies, the breaths of the Holy Spirit.

The tenth teaching in this list is “non-interference in political affairs”. Pericles praises Athens for the opposite: the citizen who takes no part in public matters is thought not unambitious but useless. Several other teachings in the list, a tribunal, compulsory education, equal rights, are public matters. How are they to be served by people who stand aside from politics?

The reading foresees “a supreme international tribunal to resolve various problems between governments and nations”. Tennyson’s young man had seen the same in a vision of 1842: battle-flags furled in a parliament of man. The poet reaches it through commerce and air war, and gives it no founder.

The reading requires religion to conform to science and reason and to hold nothing “that reason can in no way verify”. Bacon, who helped found modern science, describes the traffic the other way: a little inquiry leads from religion, deep inquiry leads back. Does the reading expect reason to prune religion, to confirm it, or both?

The sixth teaching here is to “be free of all imitations”. Emerson arrives at it as a private conviction: imitation is suicide, and each must till the plot given to him. He trusts the self to be enough; the reading frees the seeker in order to “hold fast to the foundation of divine religions”.

The reading calls all people “diverse birds” and then asks for one language, chosen or invented, so that misunderstandings may end. The Qur’an counts the difference of languages and colours among the signs of God. The reading’s universal language is a second tongue, not the only one; what would be lost if it were?

The reading names as the most distinctive new teaching “the ordination and appointment of the Center of the Covenant”. Jeremiah also expected something new under that word: a covenant unlike the earlier one, written in the heart. His has no person at its centre; the reading’s has.

“In which book is this?” the reading asks of the unity of mankind and the equality of men and women. A reader of the New Testament might point to this verse of Paul. Its unity is “in Christ Jesus”, among the baptized. Is that the same teaching, or the one the reading says no earlier book recorded?

The reading claims “special teachings”, beyond those of all the sacred books, as the spirit of this age. The Preacher denies that such a claim can ever be made: whatever is called new “hath been already of old time”. What would have to be shown for a teaching to count as new?

The reading lists side by side that religion “must be in accord with reason and science” and the “promotion of learning and spirituality”. Tennyson prays for the same pair, knowledge growing and reverence growing with it, so that mind and soul make one music. His is a hope set down in grief; the reading states it as a principle.

The first teaching in the reading is “investigation of truth”. Paul’s shortest instruction to a young church says it in nine words: test everything and keep what is good. He writes to believers about prophecies heard among them; the reading makes it the first duty of every soul.

The reading wants religion “free from blind imitations” and in agreement with science and reason. Paine made that test alone, and found that no church passed it: “My own mind is my own church.” The reading expects religion to come through the same examination as a cause of concord. What decides whether inquiry ends where Paine’s did?

The reading would have the children of all religions educated “in one school with one curriculum”. Mill, who wanted every child educated, feared exactly that when a state does it: one mould, pleasing whoever holds power. Who would write the one curriculum, and how would it leave room for the independent investigation the same list asks for?

The reading says that a religion which does not cause fellowship and love “is not religion but rather a calamity for humanity”. Pascal, a believer, had observed why the calamity is so thorough: evil is never done so completely or so cheerfully as from religious conviction.

The reading puts the educational system first among the principles and “equality of rights among the children of men” beside it. Confucius had joined the two in one sentence, twenty-four centuries earlier: in teaching, no distinction of classes.

The reading’s list sets “the protection and guidance of the Holy Spirit” next to the “independent investigation of truth”. The Buddha’s last counsel to his disciples keeps only the second: be lamps to yourselves and look to no external refuge. How does the reading hold a guidance from beyond together with a search that is one’s own?

The reading gives the equality of the sexes a reason: “mankind has two wings, male and female”. Tennyson’s prince says the same in his own figure: woman and man rise or sink together, and if she is kept small, “how shall men grow?” The poem is a courtship; the reading states a principle of religion.

The reading argues from God’s kindness to ours: “Since He is kind to all His sheep, why should we be unkind?” Malachi’s question has the same shape, from one father and one creator to the wrong of dealing treacherously with a brother. The prophet is addressing one people about its own covenant.

The reading would so adjust the economy that where a rich man has honour and affluence, “the poor man may also have a mat to lie on and a house to dwell in”. Goldsmith watched a village emptied to make one estate: wealth accumulates, he wrote, and men decay.

The reading’s aim is “the readjustment of the economic relations between the capitalists and laborers” so that each person prospers. The Manifesto addresses one of the two parties only, and tells it that it has nothing to lose. Can relations between the two be readjusted by agreement, or only, as Marx held, by the victory of one?

The reading tells missionaries that God is pleased with those “serving under a different flag and in a different camp” for the same ends. The disciples once tried to stop a man who did good but did not follow them, and were told to let him be: “he that is not against us is on our part.”

The reading says that “dead dogmas must be thrown away”. Mill explains how a dogma dies: even a true opinion, when it is no longer discussed fully and fearlessly, is held as a dead dogma. On his account the remedy is argument, not removal. Could the principles listed in this guide go the same way, repeated and never examined?

The reading calls it a crime, in the eyes of those who punished it, to have proclaimed “religious liberty, to worship God according to our own hearts”. Virginia had made that liberty law in 1786: no one to suffer for religious opinion, all free to profess and to argue it.

The reading opens with this verse of Malachi, “The Sun of Righteousness hath arisen with healing in its wings”, and addresses it to the Persians. The prophet promises the sunrise to those who fear God’s name; the reading counts its rays as oneness, love, peace and the agreement of science with religion.

The tenth of these commandments is that land may not be “bartered away nor lost to usury”, since everyone has a right to native soil. The law of Leviticus forbids the permanent sale of land for another reason, which the reading does not give: the land is God’s, and its holders are sojourners.

For an ambassador the reading reduces the Cause to a few words: pure good, mercy, truthfulness, kindness and righteousness, “and nothing more”. Micah made the best-known such reduction: to do justly, love mercy and walk humbly with God.

The reading counts among the basic teachings “association with the followers of all religions in harmony”. Paul tells the Corinthians the reverse: no yoke with unbelievers, for what has light to share with darkness? What does a community fear to lose by association, and what does the reading suppose it will keep?

The reading would “discard all such theories which cannot stand the test of intellect and empirical knowledge”. Pascal, a mathematician and experimenter, marks a limit to that test: the heart has reasons that reason does not know. The same reading asks for “heavenly Love”. By what test is that known?

“You must act in accordance with these teachings,” the reading says, having just said that Bahá’ís act in accordance with the Gospel. The letter of James makes the demand in a picture: the hearer who does not act is like a man who looks in a mirror and forgets his face.

The reading describes the faithful servant by what he is to others: a table for the hungry, water for the thirsty, healing for the sick. The parable of the judgment uses the same list, and adds that what was done for the least was done for the judge himself.

The reading’s five, “Love, work, prayer, peace and joy”, are to be realized daily. Paul’s list of the fruit of the Spirit begins with three of them, love, joy and peace. His are fruit, what grows of itself in a life; the reading’s include two things a person does, work and prayer.

Among the essentials the reading names “the abolition of the extremes of wealth and poverty”. This saying of Jesus, spoken when a costly gift was called a waste, has long been heard as a statement that poverty cannot be abolished. Is it a prediction, or, as the verse it echoes in Deuteronomy continues, a reason to open the hand?

psalm-except-the-lord.text: Except the Lord build the house, they labour in vain that build it: except the Lord keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain

corinthians-cheerful-giver.text: Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver

jeremiah-new-covenant.text: Behold, the days come, saith the Lord, that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel, and with the house of Judah … I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts; and will be their God, and they shall be my people

ecclesiastes-no-new-thing.text: The thing that hath been, it is that which shall be; and that which is done is that which shall be done: and there is no new thing under the sun. Is there any thing whereof it may be said, See, this is new? it hath been already of old time, which was before us

thessalonians-prove-all-things.text: Prove all things; hold fast that which is good

mark-not-against-us.text: And John answered him, saying, Master, we saw one casting out devils in thy name, and he followeth not us: and we forbad him, because he followeth not us. But Jesus said, Forbid him not: for there is no man which shall do a miracle in my name, that can lightly speak evil of me. For he that is not against us is on our part

malachi-sun-of-righteousness.text: But unto you that fear my name shall the Sun of righteousness arise with healing in his wings; and ye shall go forth, and grow up as calves of the stall

leviticus-land-is-mine.text: The land shall not be sold for ever: for the land is mine, for ye are strangers and sojourners with me

micah-what-doth-the-lord-require.text: He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the Lord require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God

corinthians-unequally-yoked.text: Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers: for what fellowship hath righteousness with unrighteousness? and what communion hath light with darkness? And what concord hath Christ with Belial? or what part hath he that believeth with an infidel

james-doers-of-the-word.text: But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves. For if any be a hearer of the word, and not a doer, he is like unto a man beholding his natural face in a glass: For he beholdeth himself, and goeth his way, and straightway forgetteth what manner of man he was

galatians-fruit-of-the-spirit.text: But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, Meekness, temperance: against such there is no law

matthew-poor-always.text: For ye have the poor always with you; but me ye have not always

quran-repel-with-better.text: The good deed and the evil deed are not alike. Repel the evil deed with one which is better, then lo! he, between whom and thee there was enmity (will become) as though he was a bosom friend.

analects-injury-with-justice.text: Some one said, "What do you say concerning the principle that injury should be recompensed with kindness?" The Master said, "With what then will you recompense kindness?" "Recompense injury with justice, and recompense kindness with kindness."
analects-injury-with-justice.author: Confucius

lowell-new-occasions.text: New occasions teach new duties; Time makes ancient good uncouth; / They must upward still, and onward, who would keep abreast of Truth
lowell-new-occasions.author: James Russell Lowell

thoreau-just-man-prison.text: Under a government which imprisons any unjustly, the true place for a just man is also a prison.
thoreau-just-man-prison.author: Henry David Thoreau

pericles-useless.text: Our public men have, besides politics, their private affairs to attend to, and our ordinary citizens, though occupied with the pursuits of industry, are still fair judges of public matters; for, unlike any other nation, regarding him who takes no part in these duties not as unambitious but as useless, we Athenians are able to judge at all events if we cannot originate, and, instead of looking on discussion as a stumbling-block in the way of action, we think it an indispensable preliminary to any wise action at all.
pericles-useless.author: Pericles, as reported by Thucydides

bacon-depth-in-philosophy.text: It is true, that a little philosophy inclineth man's mind to atheism; but depth in philosophy bringeth men's minds about to religion.
bacon-depth-in-philosophy.author: Francis Bacon

emerson-imitation-is-suicide.text: There is a time in every man's education when he arrives at the conviction that envy is ignorance; that imitation is suicide; that he must take himself for better, for worse, as his portion; that though the wide universe is full of good, no kernel of nourishing corn can come to him but through his toil bestowed on that plot of ground which is given to him to till.
emerson-imitation-is-suicide.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

mill-state-education.text: A general State education is a mere contrivance for moulding people to be exactly like one another
mill-state-education.author: John Stuart Mill
mill-state-education.caveat: The sentence goes on to say that such an education establishes “a despotism over the mind”. Mill would have the state require education and help to pay for it, but not provide it all.

mill-dead-dogma.text: However unwillingly a person who has a strong opinion may admit the possibility that his opinion may be false, he ought to be moved by the consideration that however true it may be, if it is not fully, frequently, and fearlessly discussed, it will be held as a dead dogma, not a living truth.
mill-dead-dogma.author: John Stuart Mill

pope-modes-of-faith.text: For modes of faith let graceless zealots fight; / His can't be wrong whose life is in the right: / In faith and hope the world will disagree, / But all mankind's concern is charity
pope-modes-of-faith.author: Alexander Pope

santayana-remember-the-past.text: Progress, far from consisting in change, depends on retentiveness. When change is absolute there remains no being to improve and no direction is set for possible improvement: and when experience is not retained, as among savages, infancy is perpetual. Those who cannot remember the past are condemned to repeat it.
santayana-remember-the-past.author: George Santayana
santayana-remember-the-past.locator: volume 1, Reason in Common Sense, chapter XII

eisenhower-every-gun.text: Every gun that is made, every warship launched, every rocket fired signifies, in the final sense, a theft from those who hunger and are not fed, those who are cold and are not clothed. This world in arms is not spending money alone. It is spending the sweat of its laborers, the genius of its scientists, the hopes of its children.
eisenhower-every-gun.author: Dwight D. Eisenhower
eisenhower-every-gun.locator: address to the American Society of Newspaper Editors, 16 April 1953

rights.note: Address by a President of the United States in office.

goldsmith-ill-fares-the-land.text: Ill fares the land, to hastening ills a prey, / Where wealth accumulates, and men decay; / Princes and lords may flourish, or may fade; / A breath can make them, as a breath has made: / But a bold peasantry, their country's pride, / When once destroyed, can never be supplied.
goldsmith-ill-fares-the-land.author: Oliver Goldsmith

tennyson-womans-cause.text: The woman's cause is man's: they rise or sink / Together, dwarf'd or godlike, bond or free: / For she that out of Lethe scales with man / The shining steps of Nature, shares with man / His nights, his days, moves with him to one goal, / Stays all the fair young planet in her hands— / If she be small, slight-natured, miserable, / How shall men grow?
tennyson-womans-cause.author: Alfred Tennyson

tennyson-knowledge-and-reverence.text: Let knowledge grow from more to more, / But more of reverence in us dwell; / That mind and soul, according well, / May make one music as before, / But vaster.
tennyson-knowledge-and-reverence.author: Alfred Tennyson

paine-own-church.text: I do not believe in the creed professed by the Jewish church, by the Roman church, by the Greek church, by the Turkish church, by the Protestant church, nor by any church that I know of. My own mind is my own church.
paine-own-church.author: Thomas Paine
paine-own-church.caveat: Paine has just said that he believes in one God and hopes for happiness beyond this life, and that religious duties consist in doing justice, loving mercy and endeavouring to make our fellow-creatures happy.

pascal-heart-has-its-reasons.text: The heart has its reasons, which reason does not know. We feel it in a thousand things.
pascal-heart-has-its-reasons.author: Blaise Pascal

jefferson-free-to-profess.text: no man shall be compelled to frequent or support any religious worship, place, or ministry whatsoever, nor shall be enforced, restrained, molested, or burdened in his body or goods, nor shall otherwise suffer on account of his religious opinions or belief; but that all men shall be free to profess, and by argument to maintain, their opinion in matters of religion, and that the same shall in no wise diminish, enlarge, or affect their civil capacities.
jefferson-free-to-profess.author: Thomas Jefferson

john-one-fold.text: And other sheep I have, which are not of this fold: them also I must bring, and they shall hear my voice; and there shall be one fold, and one shepherd

burke-cherish-prejudices.text: instead of casting away all our old prejudices, we cherish them to a very considerable degree, and, to take more shame to ourselves, we cherish them because they are prejudices; and the longer they have lasted and the more generally they have prevailed, the more we cherish them. We are afraid to put men to live and trade each on his own private stock of reason, because we suspect that this stock in each man is small
burke-cherish-prejudices.author: Edmund Burke
burke-cherish-prejudices.work: Reflections on the Revolution in France
burke-cherish-prejudices.caveat: By prejudice Burke means inherited, untaught judgment, the “general bank and capital of nations and of ages”, not hostility to a group.
